title: The Scribble on Scrabble
summary: Josh and Chuck finally tackle Scrabble, covering the rules and scoring (tile values, bingos, premium squares, mnemonic letter groups), the 1938 invention by unemployed architect Alfred Mosher Butts (originally Lexico/Criss Crosswords), James Brunot's purchase and renaming, the Macy's legend, the Selchow & Righter, Coleco, Hasbro and Mattel corporate history, competitive tournaments and the NASPA/NSA split, the early-2000s boom after the documentary Word Freaks, record-high scoring words, neuroscience and studies of scrabble players' brains, offensive slurs removed from the dictionary, cheating scandals (World Championship 2011 missing G, a teen palming blanks in 2012, Sam Kantamathi), Scrabble in pop culture, and a listener mail about mental calendar imagery.

segments.title: Opening banter and intro to Scrabble
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode, noting Josh's long campaign for a Scrabble episode, and Chuck gives a basic description of the game as a crossword-style word board game.

segments.title: Scrabble rules, tile values and mnemonics
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 15 by 15 board, the center-square start, the bingo for playing seven tiles, premium squares, letter distribution, blank tiles, and letter point values, including mnemonic groupings used by players. They also cover strategic advantages and high-value two-letter words like qi and za.

segments.title: Proper nouns, high-scoring words and foreign versions
segments.summary: Discussion of high-scoring words such as zax, zek and the highest-scoring bingo musjiks, rules about proper nouns and foreign words, house rules, and Scrabble editions in around thirty languages with different tiles.

segments.title: Foreign Scrabble editions
segments.summary: The hosts note that Scrabble has been published in about thirty languages, with some editions having extra tiles, such as double L and double R and the N with a tilde in Spanish.

segments.title: Alfred Mosher Butts and the invention of Scrabble
segments.summary: Chuck explains that architect Alfred Mosher Butts invented the game in 1938 in Jackson Heights, Queens, and that Butts first called it Lexico and Criss Crosswords without success.

segments.title: James Brunot, the rename and the Macy's story
segments.summary: James Brunot bought the rights, renamed the game Scrabble, and replaced the mental-board play with a physical board and tiles. The hosts describe his operation with his wife Helen, the factory growth, and the widely told but unverified story of a Macy's president ordering the game around 1952.

segments.title: Brunot's sale and Butts's royalties
segments.summary: Brunot sold the trademark to Selchow & Righter in 1972 for about a million and a half dollars. Butts received a small sum and royalties, and in a 1984 interview he said he was happy with his earnings.

segments.title: Coleco, Mattel, Hasbro and intellectual property
segments.summary: Coleco (Cabbage Patch Kids maker) bought Selchow & Righter in 1986 and later went bankrupt. Hasbro then took over, and Mattel won the international rights in a bidding war. The hosts muse on how licensing rights create money. Chuck and Josh then discuss pro sports TV rights and mention John Hodgman and Catherine as long-time Scrabble players.

segments.title: Competitive Scrabble tournaments and the National Scrabble Association
segments.summary: The North American Invitational tournament ran from 1978 to 2009. Selchow & Righter formed the National Scrabble Association, and later Hasbro stopped funding nationals. The North American Scrabble Players Association formed around 2009, and the nationals moved into School Scrabble.

segments.title: Scrabble boom, Word Freaks and record scores
segments.summary: The early-2000s boom is linked to the documentary Word Freaks, with tournament game numbers falling by about half by 2019. The hosts describe internal association strife and the record-high tournament scores, including oxyphenbutazone at 1,784 points (hypothetical) and cazique at 392 points.

segments.title: Neuroscience of Scrabble players
segments.summary: Studies using brain imaging found that high-level Scrabble players process words as letter shapes rather than meanings and use more spatial reasoning. Another study linked Scrabble play to closing the education gap in Alzheimer's risk, and a Russian engineering student study found students beat English teachers.

segments.title: Gender in competitive Scrabble
segments.summary: Men dominate tournament Scrabble, which the hosts attribute to earlier start ages and more anagramming and analysis rather than innate ability. Recreational play is about 60 to 40 male to female.

segments.title: Official dictionaries and removed slurs
segments.summary: The Official Scrabble Players Dictionary was released in 1978. In the 1990s, activist Judith Grad campaigned to remove slurs, and Hasbro removed them in the next edition, with a separate tournament word list (TWL98) kept for players. In 2020 further slurs were removed from tournament play. New words such as Jedi, vacs, and cuckhumber were added.

segments.title: Cheating scandals in Scrabble
segments.summary: The 2011 World Championship dispute between Nigel Richards-era rivals Chol Apoto Etri and Ed Martin over a missing G tile, which turned out to be in another player's pocket. A 13-year-old was caught palming blank tiles at the 2012 Nationals in Orlando. Sam Kantamathi was suspended for four years for cheating and faced allegations of sexual misconduct.

segments.title: John Hodgman update and Scrabble in pop culture
segments.summary: Hodgman told the hosts he and Catherine have scores in the three hundred to three-fifty range and have probably broken 400 a couple of times. Scrabble appears in Rosemary's Baby, Sinatra's Twelve Days of Christmas, Seinfeld, and Calvin and Hobbes, and led to the creation of Trivial Pursuit.

segments.title: Listener mail on mental calendars
segments.summary: A listener named Daisy from Belgium writes that she pictures the months of the year in an unusual arrangement in her head. Josh and Chuck discuss how they picture calendars.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck invite listeners to email the show and close the episode, with the standard iHeartRadio credit.
